Q: How to get __builtin_vectorelements like macro in GCC for (vector_size(bitceil(N)*alignof(T)))? A:

Short answer: there’s no direct GCC equivalent to __builtin_vectorelements.

Use sizeof(vec) / sizeof(vec[0]) for element count, or wrap it in a macro. For generic handling, combine _Generic + sizeof or rely on GCC vector extensions (__attribute__((vector_size))) and compute length manually.

Q: Laravel Component does not work on the hosting: "Undefined variable" A:

<x-navbar> will look for a Blade component named Navbar in a file named Navbar.php.

Unfortunately, Windows is case insensitive, but Linux is not. Naming the file navbar.php and the class navbar will work on Windows, but fail when deployed to a Linux webhost. (PHP's classes are case-insensitive, so navbar, Navbar, or nAvBaR will all work, but the Composer autoloader's file paths are case-sensitive if on a case-sensitive system.)

When working with Laravel, it's important to follow their coding style to avoid this issue; Laravel expects classes to use PascalCase and for file names to match. Laravel Pint can automatically resolve these and other such issues for you.

Q: Why is Signed Overflow due to computation still Undefined Behavior in C++20 A:

Based on JF Bastien's 2018 CppCon talk:

Many (most?) integer overflows are bugs—not just because they open the door to undefined behavior, but also because, even if the overflow was defined to wrap, the code would still be wrong.

Your compiler and other tools could help you find these bugs by trapping on overflow, which is allowed because overflow is UB, so the compiler can do whatever it wants. If the behavior were defined, the compiler wouldn't have the flexibility to help.

Thus the standard declares that the representation shall be two's complement. It does not define how the arithmetic operations should behave when there's an overflow because there is no good solution that works for everyone.

If the standard were to define overflow behavior, how should it define it? Many would want/expect wrapping, but others would find trapping more useful, and saturation can be useful in several domains. Since programmers can make C++ classes that behave like arithmetic types, you could have a library of integer-like types that implement whatever overflow policy you like. If you know that your code will never overflow, why should you pay the overhead of any of those behaviors?

Q: uninstall openjdk in mac A:

Legacy location

A JDK can be installed anywhere on your Mac, not just /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines.

That /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines location is legacy, dating back to when Apple directly provided an implementation of Java.

Modern locations

Now Apple is a member of the OpenJDK project. macOS is an official target platform for this open-source implementation of the Java specifications.

Many vendors provide builds/installers of JDKs for macOS based largely, if not entirely, on that OpenJDK codebase: Azul Systems, Microsoft, Amazon, SAP, BellSoft, Oracle, Adoptium of the Eclipse Foundation, IBM, Red Hat, and more. Those installers may default to some arbitrary location, or they may prompt the user to choose a folder.

Location examples:

  • If you ask IntelliJ to install a JDK for you, it goes into your_home_folder/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines.
  • If you use SDKMAN! to install JDKs, they land in your_home_folder/.sdkman/candidates/.

which java

In Terminal.app (or any such console), type and execute:

which java

You will see the path to the java executable.

Tip: I find the easiest way to locate, download, install, uninstall, and set default JDK is with SDKMAN!.
